name: Anakinra

fields.mechanism_of_action: KINERET (anakinra) is a recombinant, nonglycosylated form of the human interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra). It blocks the biologic activity of IL-1 alpha and beta by competitively inhibiting IL-1 binding to the interleukin-1 type I receptor (IL-1RI), which is expressed in a wide variety of tissues and organs. IL-1 production is induced in response to inflammatory stimuli and mediates various physiologic responses including inflammatory and immunological responses. IL-1 has a broad range of activities including cartilage degradation by its induction of the rapid loss of proteoglycans, as well as stimulation of bone resorption. The levels of the naturally occurring IL-1Ra in synovium and synovial fluid from RA patients are not sufficient to compete with the elevated amount of locally produced IL-1. Spontaneous mutations in the CIAS1/NLRP3 gene have been identified in a majority of patients with cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes such as NOMID; CIAS1/NLRP3 encodes for cryopyrin, a component of the inflammasome, and the activated inflammasome results in proteolytic maturation and secretion of IL-1beta, which has an important role in the systemic inflammation and manifestations of NOMID. DIRA is an autosomal recessive monogenic autoinflammatory disease caused by mutations in the IL1RN gene leading to loss of secretion of IL-1Ra; the deficiency of IL-1Ra results in unopposed IL-1alpha and IL-1beta pro-inflammatory signalling causing systemic inflammation with skin and bone involvement (FDA KINERET label, section 12.1).
indications: Rheumatoid arthritis: reduction in signs and symptoms and slowing the progression of structural damage in moderately to severely active rheumatoid arthritis (RA) in patients 18 years of age or older who have failed 1 or more disease modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs); may be used alone or in combination with DMARDs other than tumour necrosis factor (TNF) blocking agents (FDA KINERET label, section 1.1)
Cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (CAPS): treatment of neonatal-onset multisystem inflammatory disease (NOMID) (FDA KINERET label, section 1.2)
Deficiency of interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (DIRA): treatment of DIRA (FDA KINERET label, section 1.3)
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to E coli-derived proteins, KINERET (anakinra), or any component of the product (FDA KINERET label, section 4)

Not approved for, and not recommended for, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (JRA): safety and effectiveness in JRA have not been established and study data are insufficient to demonstrate efficacy (FDA KINERET label, section 8.4)
side_effects: Injection-site reaction is the most common and most consistently reported treatment-related adverse event: 71% of patients in Studies 1 and 4, typically within the first 4 weeks of therapy, with 72.6% mild, 24.1% moderate and 3.2% severe, lasting 14 to 28 days and characterised by erythema, ecchymosis, inflammation and pain (FDA KINERET label, section 6.1)

Rheumatoid arthritis, adverse reactions with incidence >= 5% (KINERET 100 mg/day, n=1565 vs placebo, n=733): injection site reaction 71% vs 29%, worsening of RA 19% vs 29%, upper respiratory tract infection 14% vs 17%, headache 12% vs 9%, nausea 8% vs 7%, diarrhoea 7% vs 5%, sinusitis 7% vs 7%, arthralgia 6% vs 6%, flu-like symptoms 6% vs 6%, abdominal pain 5% vs 5% (FDA KINERET label, section 6.1, Table 1)

Infections: incidence of infection 39% with KINERET versus 37% with placebo over the first 6 months; serious infections 2% versus 1% over 6 months and 3% versus 2% over 1 year, consisting primarily of bacterial events such as cellulitis, pneumonia and bone and joint infections. Patients with asthma appeared to be at higher risk of serious infections (8 of 177 patients, 4.5%) compared with placebo (0 of 50) (FDA KINERET label, section 6.1)

Serious infections: KINERET has been associated with an increased incidence of serious infections (2%) versus placebo (<1%) in RA clinical trials, and the incidence was 7% with concurrent KINERET plus etanercept versus 0% with etanercept alone (FDA KINERET label, sections 5.1 and 5.2)

Haematologic: 8% of KINERET-treated patients had decreases in neutrophil counts of at least one WHO toxicity grade versus 2% with placebo; nine patients (0.4%) experienced neutropenia (ANC < 1 x 10^9/L). Eosinophil differential percentage increased by at least one WHO toxicity grade in 9% versus 3% of placebo patients, and 2% of KINERET-treated patients had platelet decreases, all WHO toxicity grade one (FDA KINERET label, sections 5.7 and 6.1)

Malignancies: among 5300 RA patients treated with KINERET for a mean of 15 months (about 6400 patient-years), 8 lymphomas were observed (0.12 cases per 100 patient-years), 3.6-fold higher than the rate expected in the general population on the SEER database; 37 malignancies other than lymphoma were observed, most commonly breast, respiratory system and digestive system; 3 melanomas were observed in Study 4 and its open-label extension versus 1 expected case, with significance unknown (FDA KINERET label, section 6.1)

Hypersensitivity reactions including anaphylactic reactions, angioedema, urticaria, rash and pruritus; serious cutaneous reactions including drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) have been reported in patients with autoinflammatory conditions (FDA KINERET label, sections 5.3 and 6.1)

Immunogenicity: 49% of patients tested positive for anti-anakinra binding antibodies at one or more time points over up to 36 months using a biosensor assay; of 1615 patients with data at week 12 or later, 30 (2%) were positive for neutralizing antibodies, with no correlation between antibody development and adverse events (FDA KINERET label, section 6.1)
Cholesterol elevations were observed in some patients treated with KINERET (FDA KINERET label, section 6.1)

NOMID (43 patients, up to 60 months): most common treatment-emergent adverse events in the first 6 months (incidence > 10%) were injection site reaction 16.3%, headache 14.0%, vomiting 14.0%, arthralgia 11.6%, pyrexia 11.6% and nasopharyngitis 11.6%; 24 serious adverse events were reported in 14 of 43 patients, most commonly infections; 2 patients experienced neutropenia that resolved over time during continued treatment (FDA KINERET label, sections 6.2 and 5.7)

DIRA (9 patients in a natural history study, up to 10 years): the most common adverse events were upper respiratory tract infections, rash, pyrexia, influenza-like illness and gastroenteritis; 16 serious adverse events were reported in 4 of 9 patients, with infections the most common type (5 events in 2 patients); one patient had a serious event of urticaria on day 10 of treatment (FDA KINERET label, section 6.3)

Postmarketing: transaminase elevations and non-infectious hepatitis (hepatobiliary), thrombocytopenia including severe thrombocytopenia (platelet counts <10 x 10^9/L) (haematologic), DRESS, and injection-site amyloid deposits (FDA KINERET label, section 6.4)

dosage.adult: Rheumatoid arthritis: 100 mg/day administered by daily subcutaneous injection at approximately the same time each day; higher doses did not result in a higher response (FDA KINERET label, sections 2.1 and 2.4). Cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (NOMID): starting dose 1-2 mg/kg daily, individually adjusted to a maximum of 8 mg/kg daily to control active inflammation, in increments of 0.5 to 1 mg/kg; once-daily administration is generally recommended but the dose may be split into twice-daily administrations (FDA KINERET label, section 2.2). Deficiency of IL-1 receptor antagonist (DIRA): starting dose 1-2 mg/kg daily, individually adjusted to a maximum of 8 mg/kg daily, in increments of 0.5 to 1 mg/kg (FDA KINERET label, section 2.3). Severe renal insufficiency or end-stage renal disease (creatinine clearance < 30 mL/min): consider administering the prescribed dose every other day (FDA KINERET label, section 2.4). Each syringe is for single use and any unused portion after each dose should be discarded (FDA KINERET label, sections 2.2 and 2.3).
dosage.geriatric: A total of 752 RA patients aged 65 years and older, including 163 aged 75 years and older, were studied in clinical trials. No differences in safety or effectiveness were observed between these patients and younger patients, but greater sensitivity of some older individuals cannot be ruled out. Because there is a higher incidence of infections in the elderly population in general, caution should be used in treating the elderly, and the risk of toxic reactions may be greater in patients with impaired renal function because the drug is substantially excreted by the kidney (FDA KINERET label, sections 8.5 and 8.6).
dosage.paediatric: KINERET is indicated in paediatric patients with NOMID and DIRA. In the NOMID study (36 patients: 13 below 2 years, 18 between 2 and 11 years, 5 between 12 and 17 years) a starting dose of 1-2 mg/kg/day was used in all age groups, with an average maintenance dose of 3-4 mg/kg/day adequate to maintain clinical response irrespective of age, occasionally higher in severely affected patients (FDA KINERET label, section 8.4). In the DIRA study (9 patients, ages 1 month to 9 years at start of treatment) most patients received 1-2 mg/kg/day with doses up to 7.5 mg/kg/day (FDA KINERET label, section 8.4). The prefilled syringe does not allow doses lower than 20 mg to be administered (FDA KINERET label, section 8.4). KINERET is not recommended for paediatric use in juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (FDA KINERET label, section 8.4).

interactions: Tumour necrosis factor (TNF) blocking agents: use of KINERET in combination with TNF blocking agents is not recommended. In a 24-week study of concurrent KINERET and etanercept in RA, the rate of serious infections in the combination arm (7%) was higher than with etanercept alone (0%), and the combination did not result in higher ACR response rates; 2% of patients treated with concurrent KINERET and etanercept developed neutropenia (ANC < 1 x 10^9/L) (FDA KINERET label, sections 5.2 and 7.1).

Live vaccines: should not be given concurrently with KINERET. No data are available on the effects of live vaccination or the secondary transmission of infection by live vaccines in patients receiving KINERET; in a placebo-controlled trial (n=126) there was no difference in anti-tetanus antibody response when tetanus/diphtheria toxoids vaccine was given concurrently (FDA KINERET label, section 5.6).

Methotrexate: toxicologic and toxicokinetic studies in rats did not demonstrate any alterations in the clearance or toxicologic profile of either methotrexate or KINERET when the two agents were administered together (FDA KINERET label, section 7).
No drug-drug interaction studies in human subjects have been conducted for KINERET (FDA KINERET label, section 7).
fields.monitoring: Assess neutrophil counts prior to initiating KINERET, and while receiving KINERET monthly for 3 months and thereafter quarterly for a period of up to 1 year (FDA KINERET label, section 5.7). Do not initiate KINERET in patients with active infections, and discontinue it in RA if a serious infection develops; for NOMID and DIRA patients the risk of a disease flare on discontinuation should be weighed against the risk of continued treatment (FDA KINERET label, section 5.1). Health care providers should follow current CDC guidelines to evaluate for and to treat possible latent tuberculosis infections before initiating therapy, because IL-1 blockade may increase the risk of tuberculosis or other atypical or opportunistic infections (FDA KINERET label, section 5.1). Patients with DIRA should be closely monitored for allergic reactions, particularly during the first several weeks after starting treatment (FDA KINERET label, section 5.3). Rotate injection sites; in patients with confirmed injection-site amyloid deposits, monitor proteinuria for systemic amyloidosis (FDA KINERET label, section 5.5). Therapy requires clinical monitoring including complete blood counts, and assessment of hepatic and renal function is not specified for anakinra but the drug is substantially excreted by the kidney, so monitor for toxicity in renal impairment (FDA KINERET label, sections 8.6 and 12.3).
fields.patient_counselling: Advise the patient to read the FDA-approved patient labelling (Patient Information and Instructions for Use), and instruct patients and caregivers on proper dosage and administration, disposal of needles, syringes and drug product, and the use of a puncture-resistant disposal container (FDA KINERET label, section 17). The ability to inject subcutaneously should be assessed to ensure proper administration (FDA KINERET label, section 17). Infections: inform patients that KINERET may lower the ability of their immune system to fight infections and advise them to contact their doctor if they develop any symptoms of infection (FDA KINERET label, section 17). Injection-site reactions: explain that injection-site reactions may include pain, erythema, swelling, pruritus, bruising, mass, inflammation, dermatitis, oedema, urticaria, vesicles, warmth and haemorrhage; the prefilled syringe should be removed from refrigeration and left at room temperature for 30 minutes before injecting; patients should rotate the injection site and avoid injecting into an area that is already swollen or red, and report any persistent reaction to the prescribing physician (FDA KINERET label, section 17). Hypersensitivity: inform patients that serious allergic and skin reactions, including anaphylaxis, angioedema and DRESS, have been reported with KINERET (FDA KINERET label, section 17 and section 5.3). Vaccines: patients should not receive live vaccines while on KINERET (FDA KINERET label, section 5.6).
warnings: Serious infections: KINERET has been associated with an increased incidence of serious infections (2%) versus placebo (<1%) in RA trials. Administration in RA should be discontinued if a patient develops a serious infection. Treatment should not be initiated in patients with active infections, and safety and efficacy in immunosuppressed patients or patients with chronic infections have not been evaluated (FDA KINERET label, section 5.1)

Use with TNF blocking agents is not recommended because the rate of serious infections was higher with concurrent KINERET and etanercept (7%) than with etanercept alone (0%) (FDA KINERET label, section 5.2)

Hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylactic reactions and angioedema, and serious cutaneous reactions including drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) can occur; if a severe hypersensitivity reaction occurs, immediately discontinue KINERET, treat promptly and monitor until signs and symptoms resolve (FDA KINERET label, section 5.3)

Patients with DIRA may have an increased risk of allergic reactions, particularly in the first several weeks after starting KINERET treatment, and should be closely monitored during this period (FDA KINERET label, section 5.3)
Immunosuppression: the impact of treatment with KINERET on active and/or chronic infections and the development of malignancies is not known (FDA KINERET label, section 5.4)

Amyloidosis: postmarketing cases of injection-site amyloid deposits have been reported in NOMID patients after receiving high doses of KINERET injected subcutaneously into the same area of skin over long periods of time; systemic AIL1RAP (IL-1 receptor antagonist protein) amyloidosis occurred in some of these patients, who presented with proteinuria. Patients are recommended to rotate injection sites and, in patients with confirmed injection-site amyloid deposits, proteinuria should be monitored for systemic amyloidosis (FDA KINERET label, section 5.5)
Live vaccines should not be given concurrently with KINERET (FDA KINERET label, section 5.6)

Neutrophil count: patients receiving KINERET may experience a decrease in neutrophil counts; 8% of RA patients receiving KINERET had decreases of at least one WHO toxicity grade versus 2% with placebo, and nine KINERET-treated patients (0.4%) experienced neutropenia (ANC < 1 x 10^9/L) (FDA KINERET label, section 5.7)
precautions: Do not initiate KINERET in patients with active infections (FDA KINERET label, section 5.1).

Health care providers should follow current CDC guidelines both to evaluate for and to treat possible latent tuberculosis infections before initiating therapy with KINERET (FDA KINERET label, section 5.1).

Physicians should consider administration of the prescribed dose of KINERET every other day for patients with severe renal insufficiency or end-stage renal disease (creatinine clearance < 30 mL/min) (FDA KINERET label, section 2.4).

Patients or caregivers should not be allowed to administer KINERET until they have demonstrated a thorough understanding of procedures and an ability to inject the product correctly; the prescribed dose should be administered according to the instructions for use and any unused portions discarded (FDA KINERET label, section 2.5).
Rotate injection sites to reduce the risk of injection-site reactions and injection-site amyloid deposits (FDA KINERET label, sections 2.5 and 5.5).

Visually inspect the solution for particulate matter and discoloration before administration. Trace amounts of small, translucent-to-white amorphous particles of protein are normal; the prefilled syringe should not be used if the solution is discoloured or cloudy, if foreign particulate matter is present, or if the number of translucent-to-white amorphous particles appears excessive (FDA KINERET label, section 2.5).
Each syringe is intended for a single use; a new syringe must be used for each dose and any unused portion after each dose should be discarded (FDA KINERET label, sections 2.2 and 2.3).
Do not use KINERET beyond the expiration date shown on the carton (FDA KINERET label, section 2.5).

Long-term animal studies to evaluate the carcinogenic potential of KINERET were not conducted; KINERET had no effects on fertility and reproductive performance indices in male and female rats at subcutaneous doses up to 200 mg/kg/day (approximately 25 times the maximum recommended human dose on a mg/kg basis) (FDA KINERET label, section 13.1).
serious_adverse_reactions: Serious infections (2% versus <1% with placebo in RA; 7% when combined with etanercept), including cellulitis, pneumonia and bone and joint infections, and opportunistic infections with fungal, mycobacterial and bacterial pathogens (FDA KINERET label, sections 5.1, 5.2 and 6.1)
Neutropenia (ANC < 1 x 10^9/L) in nine KINERET-treated patients (0.4%), and in 2% of patients treated concurrently with etanercept (FDA KINERET label, sections 5.7 and 7.1)
Hypersensitivity reactions including anaphylactic reactions, angioedema, urticaria, rash and pruritus (FDA KINERET label, section 6.1)
Serious cutaneous reactions including drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) (FDA KINERET label, sections 5.3 and 6.4)
Injection-site amyloid deposits with systemic AIL1RAP amyloidosis presenting with proteinuria (FDA KINERET label, sections 5.5 and 6.4)
Malignancy: 8 lymphomas in 5300 patients over approximately 6400 patient-years (0.12 cases per 100 patient-years), 3.6-fold the general-population rate (FDA KINERET label, section 6.1)
Severe thrombocytopenia (platelet counts <10 x 10^9/L) and transaminase elevations with non-infectious hepatitis, reported postmarketing (FDA KINERET label, section 6.4)
fields.pregnancy_guidance: Risk summary: available data from retrospective studies and case reports on KINERET use in pregnant women are insufficient to identify a drug-associated risk of major birth defects, miscarriage, or maternal and fetal adverse events. There are risks to the mother and fetus associated with active rheumatoid arthritis or cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (CAPS). In animal reproduction studies, subcutaneous administration of anakinra to pregnant rats and rabbits during organogenesis demonstrated no evidence of fetal harm at doses up to 25 times the maximum recommended human dose. The estimated background risk of major birth defects and miscarriage for the indicated population is unknown; in the US general population the estimated background risk is 2-4% and 15-20% respectively. Disease-associated maternal risk: published data suggest the risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes in women with RA or CAPS is associated with increased disease activity, with outcomes including preterm delivery (before 37 weeks), low birth weight (<2500 g) and small for gestational age at birth (FDA KINERET label, section 8.1). Human data: an international multi-centre retrospective study reported 23 anakinra-exposed pregnancies with 21 live births of healthy infants, 1 miscarriage and 1 infant with left renal agenesis (estimated background rate of detected renal malformations 0.2-2% of all newborns); another retrospective study reported 10 anakinra-exposed pregnancies in women with CAPS with 9 live births, 1 miscarriage and 1 fetal demise in a twin pregnancy, the surviving twin being born healthy. Overall these data cannot definitively establish or exclude any anakinra-associated risks during pregnancy, and methodological limitations include small sample size and inability to control for confounders such as timing of exposure, underlying maternal disease and concomitant medication use (FDA KINERET label, section 8.1).
fields.lactation_guidance: There are no data on the presence of anakinra in either human or animal milk or on the effects on milk production. Available published data from a small retrospective study and postmarketing case reports do not establish an association between maternal anakinra use during lactation and adverse effects on breastfed infants. The limited clinical data during lactation precludes a clear determination of the risk of KINERET to an infant during lactation; therefore the developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding should be considered along with the mother's clinical need for KINERET and any potential adverse effects on the breastfed infant from KINERET or from the underlying maternal condition (FDA KINERET label, section 8.2).
fields.overdose: There have been no cases of overdose reported with KINERET in clinical trials of RA or NOMID. In sepsis trials no serious toxicities attributed to KINERET were seen when it was administered at mean calculated doses of up to 35 times those given to patients with RA over a 72-hour treatment period (FDA KINERET label, section 10).
fields.pharmacokinetics: The absolute bioavailability of KINERET after a 70 mg subcutaneous bolus injection in healthy subjects (n=11) is 95%. In subjects with RA, maximum plasma concentrations occurred 3 to 7 hours after subcutaneous administration at clinically relevant doses (1 to 2 mg/kg, n=18) and the terminal half-life ranged from 4 to 6 hours, with no unexpected accumulation after daily subcutaneous doses for up to 24 weeks. Population pharmacokinetic analysis in 341 patients showed that estimated clearance increased with increasing creatinine clearance and body weight; after adjusting for creatinine clearance and body weight, gender and age were not significant factors for mean plasma clearance. In NOMID patients at a median SC dose of 3 mg/kg once daily and median treatment time of 3.5 years, the median (range) steady-state serum exposure was Cmax 3628 (655-8511) ng/mL and C24h 203 (53-1979) ng/mL, with median (range) half-life 5.7 (3.1-28.2) hours (FDA KINERET label, section 12.3).
clinical_pearls: Anakinra is a daily subcutaneous interleukin-1 receptor antagonist protein, not an antibody: it works by blocking the IL-1 receptor rather than depleting a cytokine, so it must be given every day (FDA KINERET label, sections 2.1 and 12.1).

The most common problem is not efficacy but injection-site reaction - 71% in pivotal RA studies, typically within 4 weeks and lasting 14 to 28 days, and it was the most common reason for withdrawal from studies (FDA KINERET label, section 6.1).
The prefilled syringe cannot deliver doses below 20 mg, which matters in small children and in dose down-titration (FDA KINERET label, section 8.4).

In patients with severe renal insufficiency or end-stage renal disease (creatinine clearance < 30 mL/min) mean plasma clearance fell by 70-75% and less than 2.5% of the dose was removed by haemodialysis or CAPD, so the label advises considering every-other-day dosing (FDA KINERET label, sections 2.4 and 12.3).

Do not combine anakinra with TNF blockers: the combination roughly quadrupled the serious-infection rate (7% vs 0% with etanercept alone) without improving response (FDA KINERET label, sections 5.2 and 7.1).
Live vaccines must be avoided while on anakinra; inactivated vaccines are acceptable (FDA KINERET label, section 5.6).
DIRA patients are at increased risk of anaphylaxis in the first several weeks of therapy because they have no endogenous IL-1Ra, so early monitoring is essential (FDA KINERET label, section 5.3).

Repeated injections into the same skin site can produce local amyloid deposits with systemic AIL1RAP amyloidosis and proteinuria, so rotate injection sites and monitor proteinuria if deposits occur (FDA KINERET label, section 5.5).

The KINERET label carries no boxed warning; the key risks are serious infection, neutropenia, hypersensitivity/DRESS and injection-site amyloidosis (FDA KINERET label, sections 4, 5.1, 5.3, 5.5 and 5.7).
Anakinra is not included in the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (24th list, 2025) or the Kenya Essential Medicines List 2023, so no EML/KEML source is cited for this monograph.
fields.renal_dose_adjustment: This drug is known to be substantially excreted by the kidney and the risk of toxic reactions may be greater in patients with impaired renal function. Mean plasma clearance was reduced by 16% in mild renal insufficiency (creatinine clearance 50-80 mL/min) and 50% in moderate renal insufficiency (30-49 mL/min), and declined by 70% in severe renal insufficiency and 75% in end-stage renal disease (creatinine clearance < 30 mL/min). Less than 2.5% of the administered dose was removed by haemodialysis or continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis. Physicians should consider administering the prescribed dose of KINERET every other day for patients with severe renal insufficiency or end-stage renal disease (FDA KINERET label, sections 2.4, 8.6 and 12.3).
fields.hepatic_dose_adjustment: No formal studies have been conducted examining the pharmacokinetics of KINERET administered subcutaneously in patients with hepatic impairment, and the label specifies no hepatic dose adjustment (FDA KINERET label, section 8.7).
fields.administration_instructions: Subcutaneous injection only, once daily at approximately the same time each day. The prefilled syringe should be removed from the refrigerator and left at room temperature for 30 minutes before injecting. Wash hands, clean the injection site with an alcohol wipe and allow it to dry, pinch a fold of skin, and inject using the prefilled syringe; rotate injection sites and avoid injecting into an area that is already swollen or red. Use a new syringe for every dose, never reuse a needle or syringe, and dispose of used syringes in a puncture-resistant sharps container. Visually inspect the solution before use - trace amounts of small translucent-to-white amorphous protein particles are normal, but do not use a syringe if the solution is discoloured or cloudy or if foreign particulate matter is present. Store KINERET in the refrigerator at 2 to 8 degrees C (36 to 46 degrees F); do not freeze or shake, and protect from light (FDA KINERET label, sections 2.5, 16 and the Instructions for Use).

notes: The table stores this agent as 'Anakinra' with brand_names ['Kineret'], which matches the marketed brand KINERET (Swedish Orphan Biovitrum); brand_names has been normalised to ['KINERET']. This label is the current (10/2025 revision) KINERET prescribing information and reflects three indications - RA, NOMID and DIRA - rather than the historical RA-only indication; the class boilerplate previously on this row (including olanzapine-related antipsychotic text and a dementia boxed warning) has been superseded by this drug-specific draft. The KINERET label carries no boxed warning. Anakinra is not included in the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (24th list, 2025) or the Kenya Essential Medicines List 2023, so no EML/KEML source is cited for this monograph. Because anakinra is a daily subcutaneous protein, its practical limitations are injection-site reaction, injection burden and the 20 mg minimum deliverable dose of the prefilled syringe.
